extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (especially combinatorics and theoretical CS researchers), graduate students and authors preparing research papers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance on how to start, present, and judge mathematical research papers (especially in combinatorics/complexity), plus meta-guidance about research beliefs and how to approach conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose opening style based on story complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: If your story is very simple (e.g., 'here is a famous conjecture which we solve'), get to the point quickly; if the story is more complicated you need to prepare the reader and cannot simply 'get to the point'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct opening works when the conjecture's story has been told elsewhere; for complicated narratives use additional exposition to prepare the reader. (From 'Starting a paper is easy...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a Foreword to explain high-level philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider writing a Foreword — a paragraph or two devoted to philosophy underlying your work or a high level explanation of the key idea in your paper before you proceed to state the main result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Foreword can include motivational examples, big-picture discussion, NSF-project-outline style motivation, general physical or philosophical principles, and should be kept under one page; referees are unlikely to object. (Explicit recommendation in 'How to start a paper?')

rubrics_metrics.name: Use memorable or literary descriptions when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider putting in the Foreword some highly literary description of what you are doing; if it's beautiful or sufficiently memorable it might be quoted and bring attention to the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is optional marketing — use sparingly and keep the Foreword concise so it aids readership rather than distracts. (From 'Consider putting in the Foreword...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dull or generic opening lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't just begin with dry algebraic set-ups like 'Let A be an algebra...' — use more engaging openings when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martin Krieger's advice ('Don’t Just Begin with “Let A be an algebra…”') is cited to encourage more inviting openings that prepare readers for the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether a result should be treated as a tool or as a result in its own right
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interesting combinatorial inequality is established, choose between treating it as a tool for applications (sharpen/generalize as needed) or treating the inequality as an important object to understand, refine, and find the 'right proof' for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both sides count combinatorial objects, there is a strong urge to relate them via bijections; select the approach (tool vs intrinsic result) based on the nature and goals of the work. (From 'Proof deconstruction')

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek bijective proofs when both sides count objects
rubrics_metrics.description: When both sides of an identity or inequality count combinatorial objects, the natural criterion is to look for a direct bijection to explain the equality/inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bijection restores structure and can reveal why a result holds; this pursuit is culturally emphasized in combinatorics. (From 'Proof deconstruction' and related passages)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge combinatorics results by naturalness, examples, and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: A combinatorial theory is often judged by its examples and applications; the more natural/interesting the objects and the stronger or more elegant the final formula, the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context and applications increase perceived value; a field may be judged by its 'examples and applications' rather than abstract beauty alone. (From 'Covering all bases' and 'Is there anything new in Enumerative Combinatorics?')

rubrics_metrics.name: Value combinatorial interpretations for their explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding a combinatorial interpretation breathes life into integers arising in algebraic settings: it gives depth, structure, allows bijections, and enables analysis of positivity and asymptotics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial interpretations are sought because they relate numbers to actual combinatorial objects and permit richer study; in OPAC survey terms, a 'combinatorial interpretation' is identified with a function in #P. (From 'Combinatorial Interpretations' and earlier comments)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'combinatorial interpretation' computationally as membership in #P
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of a combinatorial interpretation as simply a function in #P: exhibiting combinatorial objects counted by the number corresponds to a polynomial-time verifiable counting relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint links combinatorial questions to complexity theory and influences what kinds of 'positive rules' one seeks for numbers like Schubert coefficients. (From 'Is there anything new in Enumerative Combinatorics?' and related passages)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and rebut potential critiques in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Write notes in a style that explains results and explicitly refutes potential critiques, addressing objections and misunderstandings head-on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's own note on Schubert positivity is written 'in a somewhat unusual style, explaining the results and refuting potential critiques' and even uses quotations to support the case — an explicit rhetorical choice when publishing controversial or delicate conditional results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance marketing/memorability against clarity and rapid communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether you want your paper to be memorable/marketed (use literary Foreword, memorable openings) or simply to communicate the result quickly; tailor the opening accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For straightforward stories prioritize clarity and brevity; for complex or broad-interest work invest in presentation and context. (Synthesis of 'Starting a paper is easy...' and Foreword advice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and revisable-ly manage your research beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: You should question your beliefs whenever possible; be willing to change your mind, try both believing and attempting to disprove conjectures, and treat different beliefs with different levels of confidence (core vs peripheral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core beliefs are rarely changed; wisdom involves adjusting belief systems to avoid contradictions as new evidence emerges. This affects research direction and how boldly you state conjectures or rely on assumptions. (From 'Faith, belief system, core beliefs' passages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complexity-theoretic evidence to assess combinatorial conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating the plausibility of combinatorial interpretations (e.g., Schubert coefficients in #P), consider complexity-theoretic placements of related decision/counting problems (e.g., whether positivity is in NP, AM, PH) as evidence for or against existence of combinatorial proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing a positivity decision problem lies in a certain complexity class (AM under GRH, etc.) informs whether a #P counting interpretation is plausible; negative placement outside PH would be strong evidence against a simple combinatorial interpretation. (From the Schubert positivity discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing conditionally (assuming hard conjectures), be explicit and defensive
rubrics_metrics.description: If your result is conditional on strong conjectures (e.g., GRH, MVA), state the assumptions clearly and explain why the conditional theorem is meaningful despite strong assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post defends its Main Theorem (Schubert positivity in NP assuming GRH and MVA) by explaining implications and answering potential critiques; rhetorical framing and transparency are recommended when relying on heavy conjectures.
